query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Ta with tungsten in the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA will enhance dynamic strain hardening and uniform plastic deformation under adiabatic high‐strain-rate loading by increasing solid‐solution strengthening and amplifying phonon drag effects. This modification is expected to delay adiabatic shear localization and improve energy absorption during impact.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA exhibiting quasi‐static properties of ~786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain, but with limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure at high strain rates.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying modification by partially substituting Ta with tungsten (e.g., a 5–10 at.% addition of W) to form a tungsten-modified HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy.
generation.conditions: Adiabatic dynamic deformation under compressive loading and impact conditions at room temperature, with strain rates in the range of approximately 1000 to 3000 s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: W addition is expected to refine the microstructure through enhanced solid-solution strengthening and promote the formation of nano-scale precipitates or modifiers that act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: W’s high melting point and its effect on increasing phonon drag will mitigate thermal softening by slowing dislocation motion at high strain rates. This will promote additional dislocation storage and an increased strain-hardening rate, delaying the onset of adiabatic shear banding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the tungsten-modified alloy is predicted to show an increase in dynamic yield strength (on the order of ~15–25% higher), an enhanced uniform plastic strain (improved uniform deformability by supporting increased plastic strain before localization), greater resistance to shear localization, and an altered impact-induced energy release profile that indicates improved energy absorption before failure.
generation.baseline: Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 with quasi-static properties of ~786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain, but limited dynamic strain hardening and rapid failure under high-strain-rate (adiabatic) conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements apply under dynamic, adiabatic deformation at room temperature with strain rates ranging from 1000 to 3000 s⁻¹. Variations in tungsten concentration or testing temperature may modify the outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in dynamic strength, uniform deformation, and energy absorption remains uncertain and will depend on the optimal tungsten content. Secondary effects on quasi-static performance and ductility also warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: (a) the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy and (b) a tungsten-modified variant with 5–10 at.% W substituting for Ta. Conduct dynamic compressive and impact tests at strain rates between 1000 and 3000 s⁻¹ under adiabatic conditions.
measurements: Uniform plastic strain (measured via stress–strain curves)
Onset and degree of shear localization (assessed by high-speed imaging and post-deformation microstructural analysis)
Impact-induced energy absorption (using energy-release measurements during ballistic impact tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the tungsten-modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dynamic yield strength, enhanced uniform plastic deformation, delayed or reduced shear localization, or improved energy absorption relative to the baseline alloy under identical testing conditions.

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity.
